To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the qPCR-based, most probable number assay for C. jejuni/C. coli on poultry products has a limit of quantification for μ ≥ 8 per 400–450 g and a limit of detection of 1–5 MPN per 400–600 g.
the qPCR-MPN protocol presented herein is a reliable method to enumerate Campylobacter in poultry products when μ > 8 cells per test volume of 400–500 g of sample.
the qPCR-MPN method is a reliable, sensitive, and specific means of enumerating Campylobacter spp. in chicken samples and that a minimum of 4 mM of sample per dilution is needed to achieve this.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the quantitation of Campylobacter on poultry products and is the first to use qPCR-based detection for the purpose of MPN determination in a multiplexed format.

the development of a rapid, sensitive and accurate method to enumerate Campylobacter in food products, and our results show that the protocol we developed can be used to quantify Campylobacter spp. in naturally contaminated chicken products.
the development and validation of a quantitative PCR-based MPN protocol for enumerating Campylobacter in poultry products.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the protocol we developed here can accurately quantify Campylobacter spp. in naturally contaminated poultry products at levels as low as 8 MPN per 400–450 g of chicken.
this qPCR-based MPN method appears to be accurate for enumerating Campylobacter at levels of 10–10,000 MPN per 400–450 g of poultry product, which is a useful range for the food industry.
the protocol presented herein can accurately quantify Campylobacter on chicken pieces with a μ > 1 using n = 6 observations per dilutions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
this qPCR-based MPN method is a viable alternative to the most widely used method, the Most Probable Number-PCR, for enumerating low numbers of Campylobacter in naturally contaminated chicken.
this protocol is useful for quantification of C. jejunium and C. coli in chicken wash samples where μ ≥ 8 cells per test volume and where n = 4 or 6 observations per diluent are used.

this qPCR MPN protocol should accurately enumerate Campylobacter in chicken at levels greater than 8 MPN per 400–450 g of sample (skin on) using a minimum of 6 technical replicates per dilution (n = 6).
The main takeaway from our work is that

one should be able to enumerate a test population of Campylobacter cells in food samples using a relatively small number of replicates (n = 6) per dilution provided one uses an appropriate test volume (V) and that the limit of detection for the protocol is not compromised by using a larger number of replicates.
one should be able to use this qPCR-based MPN protocol for quantifying Campylobacter in poultry products at levels as low as 1 to 10 cells per 400 g of product using 6 technical replicates.
the qPCR MPN method described herein is a useful tool for quantifying Campylobacter on poultry and other products where the organism is present in low numbers.
